demand.text: At the championship the robot starts at L4, splits the reef with its alliance and works down to L2, trusting the reef will still fill. Algae that gets in the way goes into the net.
The scouting paper leaves L4 out of its offensive second-pick rating because the team usually scores L4 itself.

auto.text: A Limelight estimates the pose of each coral it detects and the robot drives to them. Each auto limits the field areas where detections count, which keeps it compatible with partners a lot of the time. LEDs confirm the pivot and vision before the match.

cycle.text: The floor intake takes coral in any orientation; a ramp and indexer turn it into the end effector. One button then auto-aligns the coral score or the algae pull, while LEDs show which branch is targeted.

endgame.text: Wings steer the cage into two spinning wheels and a latch holds it; the climber pulls the deep cage back and down toward the robot's center. The championship climb takes about 10 seconds.

fallback.text: By week five, when the reef was filling, the robot's last option was to take algae off the ground and put it in the net.

gave_up.text: The architecture kept the elevator fairly narrow, so it wobbled, especially at L4 and net height. The four-bar intake absorbs frontal hits, but a single change takes about 30 to 45 minutes; the interviewed student would make it more serviceable.

changed.text: The intake was redesigned after the first event to remove an indexer dead spot. Its carbon fiber cracked at Contra Costa and was thickened. The second climber takes about 10 seconds instead of about 20.
Earlier revisions had a Rembrandts climber and a WCP end effector.
A CAN failure in Daly playoff match eight dropped the alliance to the lower bracket.

outcome.text: 57-8-0 in official play; ranked 5 of the pooled top 20 (OPR 113.54, Daly).

facts.text: 26 in by 26 in with WCP X2t modules
1/16 in pocketed belly pan with electronics on top, reached by removing a few bolts that hold the indexer
A 5/16 in pocketed 7075 plate under the elevator is also its hard stop
The voltage regulator feeds the radio and, through a power module, four CANcoders, the gyro, CANivore and beam break, so they do not flicker as the battery sags; the Limelights run unregulated

cost.text: The battery is wrestled out between intake and indexer; the indexer floor pivots up on one side, held by a zip tie on the other, after Velcro let it fall off in practice matches
With the indexer on, parts of it sometimes had to come off to reach wires; the wires were also hot glued into the PDP

solves.text: Grab coral from almost anywhere, with room for driver error, and survive frontal hits

facts.text: Takes coral from the ground in all orientations
Hit from the front, it collapses up into the robot
A ramp and flanges start turning the coral at the front of the intake
Second design, after the first competition
Bottom roller: foam over silicone tubing on a polycarbonate tube, with more tubing outside. Silicone instead of superglue cut the chunks torn out by vertical coral
Star wheel rollers run on 1/2 in hex; the team says 3/8 in would bend badly on touching coral

cost.text: Complex to service: a single change takes about 30 to 45 minutes
The carbon fiber in the middle bent and cracked at Contra Costa and was made thicker
The foam roller deformed after a few matches and intake performance fell, so four spares went to the championship; printed wheels like those of Team 5940 were not ready in time

solves.text: Remove the dead spot where coral bounced around in the larger indexer

facts.text: The ramp works with the indexer as a funnel that reorients coral into the end effector
Much smaller than the first event's version

solves.text: Fast, light lift with a low center of gravity

facts.text: 2x1 tubes, with a 2x2 tube carriage; the motor and gearbox mount below the top half of the carriage
Two Krakens with 12T pulleys drive a printed 36T pulley, a 3:1 reduction
Rope ties off with a double figure-eight knot at a standoff and large washer riveted to an aluminum tube drum
Dyneema rope, shielded by the elevator support plate and sponsor panel, replaced once in the season
An adjustable strut, and top-plate holes moved inward about 0.02 in, pinch the tubes to cut wiggle
One rope set on one side lifts it, because the short drum had to leave room for the up and down strings; no clear difference in wear between sides
The 36T pulley is Onyx with two bolts tapped in to press its layers together, and was never replaced
The up string ends on a spring at the bottom of the carriage, with a spare loop round the bolt as a failsafe; the down string ends on a shaft on the carriage
A wrench on the hex shaft tensions the cable, and a cam tensions the slotted carriage gearbox

cost.text: Kept narrow by the architecture, it wobbled a lot at L4 and net height
The rope stretched slightly and was tensioned now and then
Mounted sideways, it rocks front to back more when driving raised, which hurts accuracy at L4; new top plates removed almost all the loose fit, but the middle-stage tubes still deflect

functions.name: End effector

solves.text: Hold and score both pieces with one light mechanism

functions.type: two-sided coral and algae end effector

facts.text: One motor powers the coral side and the algae side
Two 2 in compliant wheels grip coral from the inside
Polycarbonate, MAXComposite and 3D-printed parts keep it light
Pivots on a dead-axle tube on the elevator carriage
Two absolute encoders, geared 1:1 and 41:39, give the pivot position over several turns; a jig sets their offsets

cost.text: Backlash in the printed encoder gears added a few degrees of oscillation, so the absolute encoders only set the position at start and the motor encoder runs the moves

solves.text: Reach ground algae once the reef is filling up

facts.text: On the opposite end from the coral intake; it pivots out
Two simple plates on a gearbox, in a flexible composite that takes hits while running
Takes algae from the ground into the end effector's algae side, or scores the processor

cost.text: Little used until week five, because most time went to filling the reef

functions.name: Climber

solves.text: Line up quickly and leave time for a couple more cycles

functions.type: wheel and latch deep cage climber

facts.text: Large wings guide the cage into spinning wheels, then it latches and holds to the end of the match
Pulls the cage back and down toward the robot's center
Two motors
Climb time at the championship, about
Climb time of the first version at the week 1 and 3 events, about
Gear ratio; the 125:1 in the CAD is an error
An X44 was added to it mid-season
The climb shafts are anodized 6061

solves.text: Find coral on the floor and line up on the reef without driver precision

facts.text: One camera, low on the robot, reads reef AprilTags for scoring on both branches
The other handles coral detection and auto pose estimation
All coral scores and reef algae pulls align automatically from one button
In build season the software group was creating a controller to merge Choreo trajectories with its own pure pursuit scoring
A bright white LED strip on the lower Limelight makes AprilTags easier to detect

functions.name: Driver interface

solves.text: Fit many robot functions on one controller for a single driver

functions.type: one dual-mode controller with LED feedback

facts.text: The same buttons do different actions depending on the game piece
Several scoring functions are on rear buttons so thumbs stay on the sticks
LEDs show targets and mode; an Elastic dashboard shows detail

cost.text: Dashboard logging helped cause loop overruns; moving most loggers into sendables and adjusting thread priorities reduced them

decisions.because: a hit from the front collapses it up into the robot instead of in on itself, as with some slap-down intakes
decisions.cost: a single change takes about 30 to 45 minutes

decisions.choice: Start indexing at the front of the intake
decisions.because: a ramp and flanges let the indexer be much smaller and remove a dead spot
decisions.instead_of: the first event's much larger indexer

decisions.choice: Dyneema rope to power the elevator
decisions.because: the team is most familiar with it and it is a lighter option
decisions.cost: it stretched slightly and had to be tensioned

decisions.because: it is more ductile than 6061 and no cracking was seen

decisions.choice: Limit where auto coral detections count
decisions.because: it keeps autos compatible with partners a lot of the time

decisions.choice: Build on Teams 4481 and 111 for the end effector
decisions.because: the team says the current end effector would not exist without them
it needs less reduction, keeps the center of gravity lower through the lift, and lifts less in the first half
it trades easy auxiliary ports for more usable slots, which allowed an extra climber motor mid-season; the team calls it partly a test

decisions.choice: Swap some X44 motors back to X60 before competition
decisions.because: X44s tend to overheat under load

decisions.choice: Run two robots and alternate upgrades
decisions.because: one could be used for driving and software while the other was upgraded, though both were rarely available
